episode_title: #108 Impact of Domestic Violence and Separation on the Estate Planning Process

real_qa.q: What are the key warning signs of domestic violence that estate planning lawyers should identify during client interviews?
real_qa.r: Estate planning lawyers should listen for open-ended disclosures rather than directly asking about domestic violence, as most clients do not know how to name their experience. Red flags include a client saying they have no control over finances or bank accounts, a partner doing all the talking in joint meetings, or statements like 'my partner will be furious if they find out I changed my will.' Financial abuse and coercive control are particularly difficult for clients to articulate, so practitioners should listen carefully to behavioral descriptions even if clients cannot label the abuse explicitly.
real_qa.requete: domestic violence warning signs estate planning

real_qa.q: Why should estate planning practices interview couples separately when domestic violence is suspected?
real_qa.r: Separating couple interviews prevents exposing the victim to further harm and removes the awkwardness of disclosing abuse in front of the perpetrator. By building private conversations into the standard intake process from the beginning—announced at the initial appointment call—practitioners normalize the practice so it does not appear accusatory when separation occurs. This allows clients to disclose sensitive information safely without the presence of a controlling partner.
real_qa.requete: separate interviews couples domestic violence practice

real_qa.q: How should estate planning lawyers handle communication with clients who report their spouse monitors their phone or mail?
real_qa.r: Lawyers should agree on a safe communication protocol with the client, recording preferred contact methods and identity verification details. If a client requests no voicemails because their spouse checks their phone, this must be documented visibly on the file so all staff are aware. The practice should flag the matter for controlled handling and ensure that unsafe communication channels are never used, as even one small misstep could put the client at risk.
real_qa.requete: safe communication protocol monitored phone domestic violence

real_qa.q: What additional safety assessments should estate planning lawyers conduct when a client is separating from a domestic violence relationship?
real_qa.r: Beyond updating the will, lawyers should assess who controls finances, email access, cloud storage, and other digital platforms, as abusers may retain access despite separation. Separation is both a dangerous time for victims and a complex process involving housing, parenting arrangements, property settlement, and potentially family court, magistrate court, or immigration matters simultaneously. Practitioners should recognize that clients are navigating multiple concurrent legal and safety issues and offer proactive support rather than expecting rapid responses.
real_qa.requete: separation domestic violence asset control financial access

real_qa.q: Why should all staff in an estate planning practice receive domestic violence training, not just specialized lawyers?
real_qa.r: Domestic violence indicators can emerge at any point in the client journey—from initial receptionist intake calls to document storage—and cannot fall on a single trained person. All staff should understand what to escalate and how to respond if a client discloses abuse indicators. The Queensland Law Society offers domestic violence training that general practitioners can access to recognize the behavioral and verbal cues that signal risk, allowing the entire practice to identify and protect vulnerable clients early.
real_qa.requete: domestic violence training estate planning staff receptionist

guest.bio_context: Fadzi Mambora has practical experience advising and guiding clients through domestic violence and family separation. She has worked in family and domestic violence law, and previously had an estate planning background alongside a migration lawyer, giving her cross-sectional experience in assisting clients from all different backgrounds.

real_quote: Listen, listen, listen. When clients describe domestic violence, they can explain the behaviors and what has been said, but they do not have the language to name it as financial abuse or coercive control.
key_stats: A couple married for 35 years can still experience domestic violence—length of marriage should not eliminate screening
Separation is identified as the most dangerous time for domestic violence victims attempting to reclaim their power
Queensland Law Society provides domestic violence training accessible to non-specialized practitioners
